The soft flesh ranges from orange to salmon-colored and contains abundant moisture.
A hollow central cavity holds many round, dark seeds, each surrounded by a slippery coating.

As the fruit ripens, its green skin yellows, the flesh softens, and a mild aroma develops.

Picked while mature but green, the fruit can continue ripening after harvest.
The crop grows in warm tropical and subtropical regions where freezing temperatures are uncommon.
Plants flourish in sunny sites with well-drained soil and are sensitive to frost.
On farms, fruits form along the upper trunk, beneath the plant's crown of large leaves.
Growers often treat the plant as a relatively short-lived crop because productivity can decline after several years.
The ripe flesh is commonly eaten fresh, either plain or with a squeeze of citrus juice.
Its soft flesh blends readily into smoothies, juices, and other fruit-based drinks.
Enzymes extracted from unripe fruit latex are used to tenderize meat by breaking down proteins.
The flesh contributes vitamin C and provitamin A carotenoids to meals.
